title: Representing inputs as vectors
outcome: By the end, I can explain representing inputs as vectors using a traced example and a stated limitation.
scenario: Encode the same pixel measurements in a fixed vector order.
given: Toy image features are [left_brightness, right_brightness], each = 0..10. ImageA has left2, right7; imageB has left7, right2.
All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

steps.label: Declare coordinate order
steps.detail: Coordinate0 is left brightness; coordinate1 is right brightness.

steps.label: Encode both images
steps.detail: A becomes [2, 7]; B becomes [7, 2]. Their sums match but their spatial patterns differ.

steps.label: Check input contract
steps.detail: Use the same order when training and predicting; record missing measurements rather than guessing.

explanation: A vector is an ordered list, so the position of a number carries meaning. Here the first number always means left brightness. Adding the two measurements keeps total brightness but discards which side is brighter. A network receives the representation we give it; it cannot recover a lost distinction just because it has more layers.

counterfactual.change: Swap only A’s vector order before prediction.
counterfactual.prediction: The encoded input becomes [7, 2], numerically identical to B’s original input.
counterfactual.reason: Changing coordinate order changes feature meaning even if the numbers are unchanged.

student_task: Why does equal total brightness not make A and B identical inputs? Point to the relevant step in the picture, then write the changed result and the rule or evidence that supports it.
teacher_answer: A and B place brightness in different positions. The ordered vectors distinguish left/right structure; their common sum 9 loses that distinction. Changed-case check: The encoded input becomes [7, 2], numerically identical to B’s original input. Changing coordinate order changes feature meaning even if the numbers are unchanged.
project_evidence: For your Image-pattern Network Investigation, save the input, procedure, observed result and limitation of this check. Label this worked example as practice; use a different, previously unreviewed case when checking independent understanding.
limits: These two features are simplified measurements, not a complete image representation or evidence of learned vision.
